The lighthouse at the end of the northern breakwater had not been staffed for eleven years, but the town still spoke of it as if someone lived there. Children dared each other to touch its iron door at dusk, and the older fishermen, who had once relied on its slow white sweep to bring them home through November squalls, would nod toward it whenever the weather turned. In the spring the council finally voted to sell it. The notice ran for three weeks in the local paper, between an advertisement for secondhand outboard motors and a column about the parish bake sale, and nobody expected a buyer.

The woman who answered the notice arrived on the Tuesday ferry with a canvas bag, a folding bicycle and a box of tools that she refused to let the deckhand carry. She introduced herself to the clerk as a retired surveyor and asked only two questions: whether the lamp mechanism was still intact, and whether anyone would object if she kept it running. The clerk, who had prepared a long list of answers about drainage, insurance and the right of way along the breakwater, found that she had nothing useful to say to either question.

By midsummer the light was turning again. It no longer marked anything official; the shipping lanes had moved far offshore and every trawler in the harbour carried satellite navigation. Yet on the first night it came back, half the town walked down to the seawall to watch, and nobody could quite explain why it mattered. The woman said very little about it. When a reporter from the regional station asked what she hoped to achieve, she considered the question for a long moment and then said that some things are worth maintaining simply because they were built carefully, and because letting them fail would be a small dishonesty toward the people who made them.

Why are there two high tides a day instead of one? The usual explanation begins with the Moon's gravity pulling the ocean toward it, which accounts for the bulge of water on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. The second bulge, on the opposite side, is the part that confuses most people. It does not come from some kind of push. Instead, it comes from the fact that gravity weakens with distance.

Imagine the Earth as three points along a line pointing at the Moon: the near-side ocean, the centre of the planet, and the far-side ocean. The near-side water is pulled toward the Moon slightly more strongly than the centre of the Earth, so it moves ahead of the centre. The centre, in turn, is pulled more strongly than the far-side water, so the solid Earth moves slightly away from the far-side ocean, leaving that water behind as a second bulge. What matters for the tides is not the pull itself but the difference in pull across the planet, which physicists call the tidal force.

As the Earth rotates, any given coastline passes through both bulges, which is why most places see two high tides and two low tides in a little more than twenty-four hours. The extra fifty minutes or so arise because the Moon advances along its orbit while the Earth turns, so the planet must rotate a bit further each day to catch up with it. The Sun produces tides too, roughly half as strong as the Moon's. When the Sun and the Moon line up, at new and full moon, their effects add together and produce the large spring tides; when they sit at right angles to each other, the effects partly cancel and produce the weaker neap tides. Local geography then reshapes all of this, which is why a narrow bay can see a range of fifteen metres while an enclosed sea barely notices the Moon at all.

Dear members of the allotment association,

Thank you to everyone who attended last month's general meeting, and especially to those who stayed behind to help stack the chairs. This letter summarises the decisions we reached and the work that remains before the autumn planting season.

First, the water supply. The committee obtained three quotations for replacing the corroded pipe that runs beneath the eastern path. The lowest quotation was not the most suitable, because it excluded the cost of reinstating the path surface, so the meeting agreed to accept the second quotation, which includes all groundwork and a twelve-month guarantee. Work is expected to begin in the first week of September. During that week the eastern standpipes will be switched off, and members on plots twenty to thirty-four are asked to fill their butts in advance.

Second, the waiting list. We currently have nineteen households waiting for a plot, some of them for more than two years. To shorten this list, the meeting approved a trial in which any full plot that has been substantially uncultivated for a whole growing season may be divided into two half plots. Plot holders affected by this rule will be contacted privately, and nobody will lose a plot without a conversation and a reasonable chance to explain their circumstances.

Third, the shared shed. Several tools have gone missing over the summer, and the padlock has been forced at least once. The committee will fit a combination lock and circulate the code by email only to paid-up members. Please return any borrowed equipment by the end of the month, no questions asked.

Finally, a reminder that the annual produce show takes place on the second Saturday of October. Entry forms are available from the noticeboard, and this year we are adding a category for the most unusual vegetable grown on site.

With best wishes,
The Secretary

from collections import OrderedDict
from threading import Lock
from typing import Callable, Generic, Hashable, TypeVar

K = TypeVar("K", bound=Hashable)
V = TypeVar("V")


class LRUCache(Generic[K, V]):
    """A thread-safe least-recently-used cache with a fixed capacity.

    ``get`` moves a hit to the most-recent end; ``put`` evicts the least
    recently used entry once the capacity is exceeded and reports it to the
    optional ``on_evict`` callback outside the lock.
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity: int, on_evict: Callable[[K, V], None] | None = None) -> None:
        if capacity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("capacity must be positive")
        self._capacity = capacity
        self._items: OrderedDict[K, V] = OrderedDict()
        self._lock = Lock()
        self._on_evict = on_evict
        self.hits = 0
        self.misses = 0

    def get(self, key: K, default: V | None = None) -> V | None:
        with self._lock:
            try:
                value = self._items.pop(key)
            except KeyError:
                self.misses += 1
                return default
            self._items[key] = value
            self.hits += 1
            return value

    def put(self, key: K, value: V) -> None:
        evicted: list[tuple[K, V]] = []
        with self._lock:
            if key in self._items:
                self._items.pop(key)
            self._items[key] = value
            while len(self._items) > self._capacity:
                evicted.append(self._items.popitem(last=False))
        if self._on_evict is not None:
            for old_key, old_value in evicted:
                self._on_evict(old_key, old_value)

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return len(self._items)

    def hit_rate(self) -> float:
        with self._lock:
            total = self.hits + self.misses
            return self.hits / total if total else 0.0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    log: list[str] = []
    cache: LRUCache[str, int] = LRUCache(2, on_evict=lambda k, v: log.append(f"evicted {k}={v}"))
    cache.put("a", 1)
    cache.put("b", 2)
    assert cache.get("a") == 1
    cache.put("c", 3)
    assert cache.get("b") is None
    assert log == ["evicted b=2"]
    print(f"size={len(cache)} hit_rate={cache.hit_rate():.2f}")

Theorem. There are infinitely many prime numbers.

Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, and list them as $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$. Consider the number
$$N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n + 1.$$
Since $N > 1$, it has at least one prime divisor $q$. By assumption, $q$ must be one of the $p_i$. But then $q$ divides the product $p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n$, and it also divides $N$, so it divides the difference $N - p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n = 1$. No prime divides $1$, which is a contradiction. Therefore the list of primes cannot be finite. $\blacksquare$

Remark. The argument does not claim that $N$ itself is prime. For example, with the first six primes,
$$2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509,$$
which is composite; its prime factors are simply new primes that were missing from the list.

A quantitative version. Let $\pi(x)$ denote the number of primes not exceeding $x$. The prime number theorem states that
$$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\pi(x)}{x / \ln x} = 1,$$
so the primes become rarer, but only slowly: near $x = 10^6$ roughly one integer in $\ln 10^6 \approx 13.8$ is prime. A weaker but elementary bound follows from the observation that every integer $m \le x$ can be written as $m = a^2 b$ with $b$ squarefree. There are at most $\sqrt{x}$ choices for $a$ and at most $2^{\pi(x)}$ choices for $b$, since $b$ is a product of a subset of the primes up to $x$. Hence
$$x \le \sqrt{x}\, 2^{\pi(x)}, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \pi(x) \ge \frac{\ln x}{2 \ln 2},$$
which again shows that $\pi(x) \to \infty$ as $x \to \infty$.

Problem 1. A train leaves a station at 9:00 travelling at 80 km/h. A second train leaves the same station on a parallel track at 9:45 travelling at 120 km/h in the same direction. At what time does the second train catch up with the first?

Solution. By 9:45 the first train has travelled $80 \times 0.75 = 60$ km. The second train closes the gap at $120 - 80 = 40$ km/h, so it needs $60 / 40 = 1.5$ hours. It catches up at 11:15, when both trains are $120 \times 1.5 = 180$ km from the station.

Problem 2. Solve the system
$$2x + 3y = 13, \qquad 5x - y = 7.$$

Solution. From the second equation, $y = 5x - 7$. Substituting into the first gives $2x + 3(5x - 7) = 13$, so $17x - 21 = 13$ and $x = 2$. Then $y = 5 \cdot 2 - 7 = 3$. Check: $2 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 3 = 13$ and $5 \cdot 2 - 3 = 7$.

Problem 3. A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that they have different colours?

Solution. There are $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ equally likely pairs. Pairs with one red and one blue marble number $5 \times 3 = 15$, so the probability is $15/28 \approx 0.536$.

Problem 4. Find the derivative of $f(x) = x^2 e^{3x}$ and the point where $f'(x) = 0$ for $x < 0$.

Solution. By the product rule, $f'(x) = 2x e^{3x} + 3x^2 e^{3x} = x e^{3x}(2 + 3x)$. Since $e^{3x} > 0$, the derivative vanishes at $x = 0$ and $x = -2/3$. The negative solution is $x = -2/3$, where $f(-2/3) = \frac{4}{9} e^{-2} \approx 0.0601$.

Problem 5. Compute $\displaystyle \int_0^1 x \ln x \, dx$.

Solution. Integrate by parts with $u = \ln x$ and $dv = x\,dx$, so $du = dx/x$ and $v = x^2/2$. Then
$$\int_0^1 x \ln x \, dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} \ln x\right]_0^1 - \int_0^1 \frac{x}{2}\, dx = 0 - \frac{1}{4} = -\frac{1}{4},$$
where the boundary term vanishes because $x^2 \ln x \to 0$ as $x \to 0^+$.

Le marché du samedi matin occupe toute la place de l'église depuis plus d'un siècle. Dès six heures, les maraîchers déchargent leurs cagettes de tomates, de courgettes et de haricots verts, tandis que le fromager installe sous son auvent des tommes entières et des chèvres encore humides. Les habitués arrivent tôt, avant la chaleur, avec leurs paniers d'osier et leurs listes griffonnées au dos d'une enveloppe.

Ce qui frappe le visiteur, c'est moins l'abondance des produits que la lenteur des échanges. On ne se contente pas d'acheter : on demande des nouvelles de la récolte, on discute de la pluie qui tarde, on compare la saveur des pêches de cette année à celles de l'été précédent. Le boulanger connaît le prénom de chaque enfant du quartier, et il glisse parfois un croissant supplémentaire dans le sac de ceux qui ont l'air fatigués.

Pourtant, le marché a changé. Plusieurs producteurs ont pris leur retraite sans trouver de successeur, et deux emplacements restent vides depuis l'hiver. La mairie réfléchit à un projet pour attirer de jeunes agriculteurs, notamment en réduisant le prix des places et en organisant une fois par mois une soirée de dégustation. Certains anciens s'en méfient, craignant que la place ne devienne un décor pour touristes. D'autres estiment au contraire que seule une telle ouverture permettra au marché de survivre encore cent ans.

Wer zum ersten Mal einen Sauerteig ansetzt, braucht vor allem Geduld. Man verrührt am ersten Tag gleiche Mengen Roggenmehl und lauwarmes Wasser in einem sauberen Glas, deckt es locker ab und lässt es an einem warmen Ort stehen. Nach vierundzwanzig Stunden nimmt man die Hälfte der Mischung weg und füttert den Rest erneut mit Mehl und Wasser. Diesen Vorgang wiederholt man etwa fünf bis sieben Tage lang.

Anfangs passiert scheinbar wenig, doch schon nach dem zweiten oder dritten Tag zeigen sich kleine Bläschen, und der Geruch wird deutlich säuerlich. Manchmal riecht der Teig zwischenzeitlich unangenehm, fast nach Nagellackentferner. Das ist kein Grund zur Sorge: In dieser Phase konkurrieren verschiedene Bakterien und Hefen miteinander, bis sich eine stabile Kultur aus Milchsäurebakterien und wilden Hefen durchgesetzt hat.

Ein reifer Sauerteig verdoppelt sein Volumen innerhalb weniger Stunden nach dem Füttern und riecht angenehm mild-säuerlich. Erst dann eignet er sich zum Backen. Für ein einfaches Roggenmischbrot vermengt man am Abend einen Teil des Ansatzes mit Mehl und Wasser zu einem Vorteig, lässt ihn über Nacht reifen und knetet ihn am nächsten Morgen mit Salz, weiterem Mehl und etwas Wasser zu einem festen Teig. Nach einer zweiten Ruhezeit wird das Brot geformt und bei hoher Temperatur gebacken, zunächst mit Dampf, damit sich eine kräftige Kruste bilden kann.

La biblioteca municipal abrió sus puertas en 1962 en un antiguo almacén de grano, y durante décadas fue el único lugar del pueblo con calefacción gratuita en invierno. Allí aprendieron a leer generaciones enteras de niños, y allí se reunían los jubilados cada tarde para leer el periódico y discutir sobre política con una pasión que la bibliotecaria toleraba con resignación.

Cuando llegaron las computadoras, muchos pensaron que la biblioteca perdería su sentido. Ocurrió lo contrario: la sala del fondo se convirtió en el lugar donde los vecinos aprendían a enviar correos electrónicos a sus hijos emigrados, a rellenar formularios oficiales y a buscar trabajo. La bibliotecaria, que nunca había usado un ratón, acabó dando clases los martes y los jueves, y descubrió que tenía más paciencia de la que imaginaba.

Hoy el edificio necesita una reforma urgente. El tejado tiene goteras, las estanterías de madera están combadas y el presupuesto apenas alcanza para comprar libros nuevos. Un grupo de voluntarios ha organizado una campaña para recaudar fondos, con conciertos en la plaza y una venta de libros donados. Su lema es sencillo: un pueblo que cuida su biblioteca cuida también su memoria.

中文：学习一门新语言最难的往往不是语法，而是坚持。很多人在开始的几周里热情高涨，每天背单词、听录音，可是一旦遇到瓶颈，就容易放弃。比较有效的方法是把学习融入日常生活，例如每天用新语言写三句日记，或者在做饭时听一段简短的播客。进步虽然缓慢，但只要持续积累，几个月后就会发现自己能听懂的内容明显增加了。

日本語：新しい言語を学ぶとき、大切なのは完璧を目指さないことです。間違えることを恐れて話さないでいると、いつまでも上達しません。毎日少しずつでも声に出して練習し、分からない表現があればその場で調べる習慣をつけましょう。また、好きな映画やドラマを字幕付きで見るのも、自然な言い回しを覚えるのに役立ちます。

Русский: Изучение нового языка похоже на долгую прогулку в незнакомом городе. Сначала всё кажется запутанным, улицы похожи друг на друга, и легко потеряться. Но постепенно появляются знакомые ориентиры, и однажды вы замечаете, что идёте уверенно, не заглядывая в карту. Главное — не бояться ошибок и каждый день делать хотя бы небольшой шаг вперёд.

messages.content: You are a concise, careful programming assistant.

My Python script reads a CSV with about two million rows and builds a dict from it, but it runs out of memory on an 8 GB laptop. Each row has an id, a timestamp and a short description. What can I do?

A dict of two million rows can easily take several gigabytes in Python, because every string, integer and tuple is a separate object with its own overhead. A few options, roughly in order of effort:

1. Stream instead of loading everything. If you only need aggregates (counts, sums, the latest timestamp per id), iterate over the file with the csv module and update small accumulators as you go.
2. Keep only the columns you need. If the description is rarely used, leave it out of the dict or store it on disk.
3. Use a columnar library. pandas or polars can read the file with explicit dtypes, for example int64 for the id and datetime64 for the timestamp, which typically uses a fraction of the memory of Python objects.
4. Put it in SQLite. Importing the CSV into a SQLite database gives you indexed lookups by id with almost no memory use.

What do you do with the dict after building it?
I need to look up the description for an id many times during a later processing step, in random order.

Then an indexed on-disk store is the best fit, because random lookups are exactly what an index is for, and you avoid holding two million descriptions in memory. With SQLite it looks like this:

```python
import csv
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect("rows.db")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS rows (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ts TEXT, description TEXT)")
with open("data.csv", newline="") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    next(reader)  # skip the header
    con.executemany("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO rows VALUES (?, ?, ?)", reader)
con.commit()

def description(row_id):
    hit = con.execute("SELECT description FROM rows WHERE id = ?", (row_id,)).fetchone()
    return hit[0] if hit else None
```

Because id is the primary key, each lookup is a B-tree search that touches only a few pages, and SQLite's page cache keeps frequently used pages in memory automatically. The import runs once; later runs can reuse rows.db directly. If lookups turn out to be the bottleneck, wrap them in a functools.lru_cache or batch several ids into one query with an IN clause.
I'm planning a four-day trip to a mountain town in late October. I like hiking but I'm worried about the weather. Any advice on what to pack and how to plan the days?

Late October in the mountains can mean anything from crisp sunny days to sleet, so plan for flexibility rather than for one forecast.

Packing: dress in layers. A moisture-wicking base layer, a warm fleece or light down jacket, and a waterproof, windproof shell will cover most conditions. Add a hat and gloves even if the forecast looks mild, because temperatures drop quickly once the sun goes behind a ridge. Waterproof hiking boots that are already broken in matter more than any other single item. Pack a headlamp too: days are short, and it is easy to misjudge how long a descent will take.

Planning the days: check the forecast each evening and keep two or three hikes of different lengths in mind. Use the clearest day for the longest or highest route, and keep a shorter valley walk or a town day for rain. Start early, aim to be back well before sunset, and look up whether any high trails or lifts close for the season at the end of October. Finally, tell someone at your accommodation where you are going each day; it costs nothing and helps a great deal if something goes wrong.
Explain technical ideas clearly to curious non-specialists.
What is the difference between a virus and a bacterium, and why don't antibiotics work against viruses?

Bacteria are complete living cells. Each one has its own membrane, its own machinery for turning food into energy, and ribosomes for building proteins, and it can reproduce by itself by dividing in two. Many bacteria are harmless or even helpful, like those in your gut, and only some cause disease.

Viruses are much smaller and far simpler. A virus is essentially a set of genetic instructions, made of DNA or RNA, wrapped in a protein coat and sometimes an outer envelope. It has no metabolism of its own and cannot reproduce on its own. To multiply, it has to get inside a host cell and hijack that cell's machinery to copy itself.

Antibiotics work by attacking structures or processes that bacteria have and our own cells do not, or have in a different form. Penicillin, for example, blocks the construction of the bacterial cell wall, and other antibiotics jam bacterial ribosomes. Viruses have no cell wall and no ribosomes of their own, so these drugs have nothing to hit. That is why doctors use different tools against viruses: vaccines that train the immune system in advance, and antiviral drugs that target specific steps of a particular virus's life cycle, such as the enzyme it uses to copy its genetic material.
